catalog_quote: Thiessen sets out to reconstruct the sound system and a corpus of 165 etyma for the parent language of seven speech varieties spoken on Palawan. He also puts forward a subgrouping based on the evidence of phonological innovations, yielding a North Palawan (Batak and Aborlan Tagbanwa) and a South Palawan (Quezon, Brooke's Point, Canipaan, Tau't Batu, and Molbog). ... Accent is not marked because it is purportedly not phonemic, although the author's statement of this is somewhat confusing: 'Word accent in Q[uezon], B[rooke's] P[oint], C[anipaan], and M[olbog] falls on one of the last two syllables of a word, including both suffixed and unsuffixed forms. . . In none of the languages are words distinguished by accent alone so accent is not contrastive on this level and is not written' (10). The quoted passage is there verbatim: the paragraph beginning 'Thiessen sets out to reconstruct the sound system and a corpus of 165 etyma for the parent language of seven speech varieties spoken on Palawan.. a South Palawan (Quezon, Brooke's Point, Canipaan, Tau't Batu, and Molbog)', and further down 'Accent is not marked because it is purportedly not phonemic, although the author's statement of this is somewhat confusing: 'Word accent in Q[uezon], B[rooke's] P[oint], C[anipaan], and M[olbog] falls on one of the last two syllables of a word, in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Thiessen (second-hand): in none of his seven Palawan varieties, Tau't Batu included, are words distinguished by accent alone, so accent is non-contrastive and left unwritten; the explicit 'falls on one of the last two syllables' clause names Quezon, Brooke's Point, Canipaan and Molbog, and whatever Thiessen said about Tau't Batu (and Batak/Aborlan) in the elided passage is not recoverable from the review. Revel 1995 gives penultimate stress for Palawan as a whole, of which Tau't Bato is a subgroup, but not from Singnapan data.
new_statements.exceptions: Zorc notes the statement is ambiguous between regular penult, regular ultima, or sporadic placement, cites Warren 1959 Batak minimal pairs contradicting non-contrastiveness for Batak, and attributes modern accent contrasts on Palawan to Tagalog/Bisayan superstrata varying by idiolect.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, suffixed and unsuffixed forms (per Thiessen's wording); wordlist/etyma citation forms; accent not transcribed in the data.
new_statements.identity_note: Taut Batu (taut1234) = Tau't Batu / Tau't Bato / Taaw't Bato, an exonym (1978) for the Palawan-speaking group of Singnapan valley, Barangay Ransang, Rizal (formerly Quezon), SW Palawan. Glottolog keeps it as a separate Southern Palawanic language on the strength of Thiessen 1980; Revel and most ethnographers treat it as a subgroup/dialect of Palawan(o) (cf. Southwest Palawano plv sout2905 / Central Palawano plc cent2091 / Brooke's Point plw broo1239). The quoted accent statement is Thiessen's for his whole seven-variety Palawan sample; the explicit final-two-syllable clause names Quezon, Brooke's Point, Canipaan and Molbog, not Tau't Batu. Revel 1995's 'penultimate stress' describes Palawan generally from Brooke's Point highland data.

sources.note: p.109: Thiessen's seven varieties include Tau't Batu; Zorc quotes Thiessen 1981 p.10 verbatim: word accent in Quezon, Brooke's Point, Canipaan and Molbog falls on one of the last two syllables; 'In none of the languages are words distinguished by accent alone so accent is not contrastive.. and is not written'. Zorc adds that accent is unmarked in Thiessen's data, finds the statement ambiguous (penult-regular vs ultima-regular vs sporadic), and argues Proto-Palawan had lost PPH accent, with modern contrasts due to Tagalog/Bisayan superstrata.
